2.1 **The case $A_2$: the positive roots.** By 1.1, the three vectors $e_s=\rho(1)e_s$, $e_t=\rho(1)e_t$ and $e_s+e_t=\rho(t)e_s$ are roots; they lie in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$, hence in $\Phi_+$, and they are pairwise distinct as functions on $\{s,t\}$, with values $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$. By [F6] the six chambers are cut out by the three root hyperplanes $H_\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$; the map $\alpha\mapsto H_\alpha$ from $\Phi_+$ onto these lines is injective, because two roots on one line are proportional and both have $B$-norm one by [F2], forcing the proportionality factor to be $\pm1$, and it is surjective because every $H_\beta$ equals $H_{-\beta}$ with exactly one of $\pm\beta$ in $\Phi_+$. Hence $|\Phi_+|=3$ and $\Phi_+=\{e_s,\,e_t,\,e_s+e_t\}$. [F2, F6, step 1.1]

2.2 **The case $A_2$: the chambers.** Write $y_s:=f(e_s)$ and $y_t:=f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $f$ is described by the pair $(y_s,y_t)$. By [F6], $f\in wC^\circ$ if and only if $f(\rho(w)e_s)>0$ and $f(\rho(w)e_t)>0$. Using the products $\rho(s)e_s=-e_s$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$, $\rho(t)e_t=-e_t$, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$ from [F1] and 1.1, together with $\rho(st)e_s=e_t$, $\rho(st)e_t=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_s=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_t=e_s$, $\rho(sts)e_s=-e_t$, $\rho(sts)e_t=-e_s$ (computed from $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$), this gives $C^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_t>0\}$, $sC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$, $stC^\circ=\{y_t>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$, $stsC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_t<0\}=-C^\circ$, $tsC^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$ and $tC^\circ=\{y_t<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$. On each of these six sets the signs of $(y_s,\,y_t,\,y_s+y_t)$ are the six distinct patterns $(+,+,+)$, $(-,+,+)$, $(-,+,-)$, $(-,-,-)$, $(+,-,-)$, $(+,-,+)$; these are exactly the six combinations not excluded by one of the three equations $y_s=0$, $y_t=0$, $y_s+y_t=0$, so the six chambers are the six sectors, in the stated cyclic order. By [F5], $s^2=t^2=1$ and $(st)^3=1$ give $s(st)^j=(ts)^js$ and $t(st)^j=(ts)^jt$ for all $j\ge0$ and $(ts)^j=(st)^{-j}$, whence $su_k=u_{1-k}$ and $tu_k=u_{-1-k}$ with indices read modulo $6$; combined with $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,6-k)$ this gives $\ell(su_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\ell(tu_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$. By the shortening equivalence of [F6], $H_{e_s}$ separates $C^\circ$ from $u_1C^\circ,u_2C^\circ,u_3C^\circ$ and $H_{e_t}$ from $u_3C^\circ,u_4C^\circ,u_5C^\circ$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.2 **The case $I_2(5)$: the positive roots.** By 2.3 and [F1], $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, and using $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$ one computes $\rho(st)e_s=\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=-e_s+\phi(e_t+\phi e_s)=(\phi^2-1)e_s+\phi e_t=\phi(e_s+e_t)$. Hence the five vectors $e_s=\rho(1)e_s$, $e_t=\rho(1)e_t$, $e_t+\phi e_s=\rho(s)e_t$, $e_s+\phi e_t=\rho(t)e_s$ and $\phi(e_s+e_t)=\rho(st)e_s$ are roots; each lies in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$, so all five lie in $\Phi_+$, and they are pairwise distinct as functions on $\{s,t\}$, with values $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(\phi,1)$, $(1,\phi)$, $(\phi,\phi)$. By [F6] the ten chambers are cut out by the five root hyperplanes $H_\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$, and as in 2.1 the map $\alpha\mapsto H_\alpha$ is a bijection from $\Phi_+$ onto these lines, so $|\Phi_+|=5$ and the five listed vectors exhaust $\Phi_+$; each of them has $B$-norm one because it is a root, by [F2]. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.3, algebra]

6.1 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the chambers.** Let $\delta(f):=f(e_s)+f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $\delta(f)=f(u)$; since $\rho(w)u=u$ for all $w$ by 1.3, the value $\delta(f)$ is preserved by the dual action: $\delta(w\cdot f)=(w\cdot f)(u)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}u)=f(u)=\delta(f)$. On $L:=\{f:\delta(f)=1\}$ with coordinate $y_s=f(e_s)$, $C^\circ$ has trace $(0,1)$. By [F1] and the dual action in [F6], $s$ acts by $y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t$ by $y_s\mapsto2-y_s$; hence $st$ acts by translation $y_s\mapsto y_s-2$. It follows that $(st)^kC^\circ\cap L=(-2k,1-2k)$ and $(st)^ksC^\circ\cap L=(-2k-1,-2k)$ for every integer $k$. These are all intervals $(j,j+1)$, and all group elements are alternating words by [F5] (cancelling adjacent equal letters); therefore these are exactly the open chamber traces, and no integer point belongs to one. Every chamber is a nonempty cone contained in $\{\delta>0\}$, since this holds for $C^\circ$ and $\delta$ is invariant. Each chamber $K$ equals the cone $\{\lambda x:\lambda>0,\ x\in K\cap L\}$ over its trace, because for $f\in K$ its normalisation $f/\delta(f)$ lies in $K\cap L$ and $f=\delta(f)\,(f/\delta(f))$ with $\delta(f)>0$; hence the chambers are exactly the cones over the intervals $(j,j+1)$. Finally $H_{e_s}\cap L$ is the point with $y_s=0$, and $H_{e_t}\cap L$ is the point with $y_s=1$, because $y_t=1-y_s$ on $L$. Together with 1.1-1.3, 2.1-2.5, 3.1-3.2, 4.1 and 5.1 this verifies all the claims of (i), (ii) and (iii). [F1, F5, F6, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

changed_supplier_uses.supplier_clause_check: Definition(1) uses the LEFT rho action to define N(w)=positive roots sent negative; clause(2) explicitly proves inverse/sign/simple-reflection recursion using current root-sign(3)/root-length(1), not an unproved cardinality. Clause(3) distinguishes suffix roots N(w) from prefix roots N(w^-1) and defers exactness/distinctness to the inversion theorem. Foundational reflection/form deps are context, not extra faithfulness claims.
citation_contexts: Let $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m:=m(s,t)\in\{3,5,\infty\}$, $V=\mathbb R^S$, and let $B$ be the Coxeter form with $c=\cos(\pi/m)$ for $m<\infty$ and $c=1$ for $m=\infty$, so that $B(e_s,e_s)=B(e_t,e_t)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-c$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]). Let $\rho,\Phi,\Phi_\pm,N,C^\circ,W,\ell$ be as on this page ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]], [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]], [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]]), and let $u_k$ denote the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters. The following data are computed and verified.

**Given:** a two-element set $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m:=m(s,t)\in\{3,5,\infty\}$, the space $V=\mathbb R^S$ with basis vectors $e_s,e_t$, the Coxeter form $B$ with constant $c$ ($c=\cos(\pi/m)$ for $m<\infty$, $c=1$ for $m=\infty$), the presented Coxeter group $W$ with length function $\ell$, the canonical reflection homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ with root system $\Phi$, the partition $\Phi=\Phi_+\sqcup\Phi_-$, the inversion sets $N(w)$ of [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]], and the alternating words $u_k=s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters beginning with $s$.

[F3] $N(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:\rho(w)\alpha\in\Phi_-\}$ for $w\in W$; $N(1)=\emptyset$; and for $u\in W$, $r\in\{s,t\}$ with $\ell(ur)>\ell(u)$ one has $N(ur)=\{e_r\}\sqcup\rho(r)N(u)$, while for $\ell(ur)<\ell(u)$ one has $N(ur)=\rho(r)(N(u)\setminus\{e_r\})$, where $\rho(r)N(u)=\{\rho(r)\beta:\beta\in N(u)\}$ ([[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]] (1), (2)).

proof_uses.text: 2.5 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the inversion sets.** By [F5] the $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell(u_k)=k$, and $u_{2k}=(st)^k$, $u_{2k+1}=(st)^ks$. We prove by induction on $k\ge0$ the two formulas $N((st)^k)=\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le 2k-1\}$ and $N((st)^ks)=\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le 2k\}$. For $k=0$ the first is $N(1)=\emptyset$ and the second is $N(s)=\{e_s\}$. Assume the second formula for some $k\ge0$. Since $\ell((st)^{k+1})=2k+2>2k+1=\ell((st)^ks)$, the recursion of [F3] gives $N((st)^{k+1})=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N((st)^ks)$; by 1.3, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+2e_t=u+e_t$, so $\rho(t)\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le2k\}=\{ju+u+e_t:0\le j\le2k\}=\{(j+1)u+e_t:0\le j\le2k\}$ and therefore $N((st)^{k+1})=\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le2k+1\}$, which is the first formula with $k+1$. Since $\ell((st)^{k+1}s)=2k+3>2k+2=\ell((st)^{k+1})$, again, but with $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+2e_s=u+e_s$ from 1.3, $N((st)^{k+1}s)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le2k+1\}=\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le2k+2\}$, the second formula with $k+1$. So both formulas hold for all $k\ge0$. Their elements are pairwise distinct because $u\ne0$, so the two sets have cardinalities $2k$ and $2k+1$, equal to $\ell((st)^k)=2k$ and $\ell((st)^ks)=2k+1$ by [F5], in agreement with [F4]. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 **The case $A_2$: the inversion sets.** By [F3] and 1.1, and since $\ell(u_0)=0<\ell(u_1)=1<\ell(u_2)=2<\ell(u_3)=3$ by [F5], one has $N(s)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(1)=\{e_s\}$, $N(t)=\{e_t\}$, $N(st)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(s)=\{e_t,\,e_s+e_t\}$, $N(ts)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(t)=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t\}$ and $N(sts)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(st)=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t,\,\rho(s)(e_s+e_t)\}=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t,\,e_t\}=\Phi_+$, where we used $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$ and $\rho(s)(e_s+e_t)=\rho(s)e_s+\rho(s)e_t=-e_s+(e_s+e_t)=e_t$; also $N(1)=\emptyset$. The cardinalities $0,1,1,2,2,3$ equal $\ell(1),\ell(s),\ell(t),\ell(st),\ell(ts),\ell(sts)$ by [F5], as asserted. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 **The case $I_2(5)$: the inversion sets $N(u_k)$, $1\le k\le5$.** By [F5], $\ell(u_k)=k$ for $1\le k\le5$, so each step below is a shortening-free step of the recursion of [F3] and the union is disjoint. Starting from $N(1)=\emptyset$ and using the reflection values $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$, $\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=\phi(e_s+e_t)$, $\rho(t)(e_t+\phi e_s)=\phi(e_s+e_t)$, $\rho(t)\phi(e_s+e_t)=\phi e_s+e_t$ and $\rho(s)\phi(e_s+e_t)=e_s+\phi e_t$ (all from [F1], $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$) one computes $N(u_1)=\{e_s\}$, $N(u_2)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(u_1)=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t\}$, $N(u_3)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_2)=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s,\ \phi(e_s+e_t)\}$, $N(u_4)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(u_3)=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ \phi(e_s+e_t),\ e_t+\phi e_s\}$ and $N(u_5)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_4)=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s,\ \phi(e_s+e_t),\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ e_t\}=\Phi_+$, the last equality by 3.2. This gives the displayed sets $N(u_1),\dots,N(u_5)$, of cardinalities $k=|N(u_k)|=\ell(u_k)$ as required by [F4]. [F3, F4, F5, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 **The case $I_2(5)$: the inversion sets $N(u_k)$, $5\le k<10$.** Since $N(u_5)=\Phi_+$ by 4.1, the reflection $\rho(u_5)$ maps $\Phi_+$ bijectively onto $\Phi_-$ (as $N(u_5)=\Phi_+$ means $\rho(u_5)\Phi_+\subseteq\Phi_-$, and $\rho(u_5)$ induces a bijection of $\Phi$); hence for $\alpha\in\Phi_+$: $\alpha\in N(u_5w)$ if and only if $\rho(w)\alpha\in\Phi_+$, because $\rho(u_5)$ maps $\Phi_+$ onto $\Phi_-$ and $\Phi_-$ onto $\Phi_+$. Comparing with the definition of $N(w)$ this gives $N(u_5w)=\Phi_+\setminus N(w)$ for every $w\in W$. For $5\le k<10$ one has $u_k=u_5\,u_{k-5}'$, where $u_j'$ is the alternating word of length $j$ beginning with $t$; hence $N(u_k)=\Phi_+\setminus N(u_{k-5}')$. In particular $N(u_6)=\Phi_+\setminus\{e_t\}$ and, using the recursion of [F3] once more for $u_2'=ts$ (read with the roles of $s$ and $t$ exchanged, $\ell(u_2')=2>\ell(t)=1$), $N(u_2')=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_1')=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s\}$, so that $N(u_7)=\Phi_+\setminus N(u_2')=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ \phi(e_s+e_t)\}$, of cardinality $3=\ell(u_7)$. [F3, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

changed_supplier_uses.supplier_clause_check: Definition(1)-(3): finite real coordinate space, symmetric Gram B_ii=1/B_st=-cos(pi/m) (=-1 at infinity), r_a only when B(a,a)!=0; no global definiteness or nondegeneracy.
citation_contexts: Let $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m:=m(s,t)\in\{3,5,\infty\}$, $V=\mathbb R^S$, and let $B$ be the Coxeter form with $c=\cos(\pi/m)$ for $m<\infty$ and $c=1$ for $m=\infty$, so that $B(e_s,e_s)=B(e_t,e_t)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-c$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]]). Let $\rho,\Phi,\Phi_\pm,N,C^\circ,W,\ell$ be as on this page ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[thm-cg-root-sign-and-simple-reflection-positivity]], [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]], [[thm-cg-root-inversion-formulas-and-strong-exchange]]), and let $u_k$ denote the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters. The following data are computed and verified.

[F1] $B(e_s,e_s)=B(e_t,e_t)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-c$; the reflection $r_a$ with normal $a$, $B(a,a)\ne0$, is $r_a(v)=v-\frac{2B(v,a)}{B(a,a)}a$, so that $r_s(e_s)=-e_s$, $r_s(e_t)=e_t+2ce_s$ and $r_t(e_t)=-e_t$, $r_t(e_s)=e_s+2ce_t$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.1 **The case $A_2$: the constant.** Put $x:=\pi/3$, $q:=\cos x$ and $r:=\sin x$. The addition formulas give $\cos 2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2q^2-1$ and $\sin 2x=2qr$, hence $\cos 3x=\cos(2x+x)=(2q^2-1)q-(2qr)r=2q^3-q-2q(1-q^2)=4q^3-3q$; since $3x=\pi$ and $\cos\pi=-1$, we get $4q^3-3q+1=0$, that is $(q+1)(2q-1)^2=0$. Now $0<\pi/3<\pi/2<\pi$ and cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos 0=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, so $0<q<1$; hence $q\ne-1$ and $q=1/2$. Thus in this case $c=1/2$, and the reflection formulas of [F1] give $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$. [F1, F7, algebra]

1.3 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the invariant functional direction.** Here $c=1$, so $B(u,u)=B(e_s,e_s)+2B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=1-2+1=0$, $B(u,e_s)=B(e_s,e_s)+B(e_t,e_s)=1-1=0$ and $B(u,e_t)=B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=-1+1=0$, where $u:=e_s+e_t$; by bilinearity $B(u,\cdot)=0$ on $\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$. Moreover $\rho(s)u=\rho(s)e_s+\rho(s)e_t=-e_s+(e_t+2e_s)=u$ and $\rho(t)u=(e_s+2e_t)-e_t=u$, so $\rho(w)u=u$ for every $w\in W$, because $W$ is generated by $s,t$ and $\rho$ is a homomorphism. [F1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.2 **The case $A_2$: the chambers.** Write $y_s:=f(e_s)$ and $y_t:=f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $f$ is described by the pair $(y_s,y_t)$. By [F6], $f\in wC^\circ$ if and only if $f(\rho(w)e_s)>0$ and $f(\rho(w)e_t)>0$. Using the products $\rho(s)e_s=-e_s$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$, $\rho(t)e_t=-e_t$, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$ from [F1] and 1.1, together with $\rho(st)e_s=e_t$, $\rho(st)e_t=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_s=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_t=e_s$, $\rho(sts)e_s=-e_t$, $\rho(sts)e_t=-e_s$ (computed from $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$), this gives $C^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_t>0\}$, $sC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$, $stC^\circ=\{y_t>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$, $stsC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_t<0\}=-C^\circ$, $tsC^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$ and $tC^\circ=\{y_t<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$. On each of these six sets the signs of $(y_s,\,y_t,\,y_s+y_t)$ are the six distinct patterns $(+,+,+)$, $(-,+,+)$, $(-,+,-)$, $(-,-,-)$, $(+,-,-)$, $(+,-,+)$; these are exactly the six combinations not excluded by one of the three equations $y_s=0$, $y_t=0$, $y_s+y_t=0$, so the six chambers are the six sectors, in the stated cyclic order. By [F5], $s^2=t^2=1$ and $(st)^3=1$ give $s(st)^j=(ts)^js$ and $t(st)^j=(ts)^jt$ for all $j\ge0$ and $(ts)^j=(st)^{-j}$, whence $su_k=u_{1-k}$ and $tu_k=u_{-1-k}$ with indices read modulo $6$; combined with $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,6-k)$ this gives $\ell(su_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\ell(tu_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$. By the shortening equivalence of [F6], $H_{e_s}$ separates $C^\circ$ from $u_1C^\circ,u_2C^\circ,u_3C^\circ$ and $H_{e_t}$ from $u_3C^\circ,u_4C^\circ,u_5C^\circ$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.4 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the positive roots.** Put $\Psi:=\{e_s+ku:k\ge0\}\cup\{e_t+ku:k\ge0\}$. First, $\Psi\subseteq\Phi_+$: clearly $e_s,e_t\in\Psi\cap\Phi_+$, and for $k\ge1$ the identities $e_s+ku=\rho(s)(e_t+(k-1)u)$ and $e_t+ku=\rho(t)(e_s+(k-1)u)$ hold by 1.3, so induction on $k$ shows that every element of $\Psi$ is a root; every element of $\Psi$ has nonnegative coefficients in $e_s,e_t$, so $\Psi\subseteq\Phi\cap V_+\setminus\{0\}=\Phi_+$. Conversely, $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$ is stable under $\rho(s)$ and $\rho(t)$: by 1.3 one has $\rho(s)(e_s+ku)=-e_s+ku$, which is $e_t+(k-1)u$ for $k\ge1$ and $-e_s$ for $k=0$; $\rho(s)(e_t+ku)=(e_t+2e_s)+ku=e_s+(k+1)u$; $\rho(t)(e_t+ku)=-e_t+ku$, which is $e_s+(k-1)u$ for $k\ge1$ and $-e_t$ for $k=0$; and $\rho(t)(e_s+ku)=(e_s+2e_t)+ku=e_t+(k+1)u$. Since $W$ is generated by $s,t$ and $\rho$ is a homomorphism, $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$ is stable under every $\rho(w)$; it contains $e_s,e_t$, so it contains the orbit $\Phi$. Hence $\Phi\subseteq\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$, and an element of $\Phi_+$ lies in $\Psi$: it lies in $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$, and no element of $-\Psi$ has all coefficients nonnegative, while the elements of $V_+$ do. Therefore $\Phi_+=\Psi$; finally the two families $e_s+ku$ and $e_t+ku$ are disjoint and each is injective in $k$, because $u\ne0$ while evaluating $e_s+ku=e_s+k'u$ at $s$ gives $k=k'$, and $e_s+ku=e_t+k'u$ would give $1+k=k'$ at $s$ and $k=1+k'$ at $t$, hence $k=k+2$, a contradiction; so $\Phi_+$ is infinite. [F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.2 **The case $I_2(5)$: the positive roots.** By 2.3 and [F1], $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, and using $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$ one computes $\rho(st)e_s=\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=-e_s+\phi(e_t+\phi e_s)=(\phi^2-1)e_s+\phi e_t=\phi(e_s+e_t)$. Hence the five vectors $e_s=\rho(1)e_s$, $e_t=\rho(1)e_t$, $e_t+\phi e_s=\rho(s)e_t$, $e_s+\phi e_t=\rho(t)e_s$ and $\phi(e_s+e_t)=\rho(st)e_s$ are roots; each lies in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$, so all five lie in $\Phi_+$, and they are pairwise distinct as functions on $\{s,t\}$, with values $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(\phi,1)$, $(1,\phi)$, $(\phi,\phi)$. By [F6] the ten chambers are cut out by the five root hyperplanes $H_\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$, and as in 2.1 the map $\alpha\mapsto H_\alpha$ is a bijection from $\Phi_+$ onto these lines, so $|\Phi_+|=5$ and the five listed vectors exhaust $\Phi_+$; each of them has $B$-norm one because it is a root, by [F2]. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 **The case $I_2(5)$: the inversion sets $N(u_k)$, $1\le k\le5$.** By [F5], $\ell(u_k)=k$ for $1\le k\le5$, so each step below is a shortening-free step of the recursion of [F3] and the union is disjoint. Together with 1.1-1.3, 2.1-2.5, 3.1-3.2, 4.1 and 5.1 this verifies all the claims of (i), (ii) and (iii). [F1, F5, F6, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

citation_contexts: [F5] In $W$ one has $s^2=t^2=1$ and, when $m<\infty$, $(st)^m=1$; if $m<\infty$ the elements $u_0,\dots,u_{2m-1}$ exhaust $W$ and $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,2m-k)$; if $m=\infty$ the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell(u_k)=k$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-cg-rank-two-prefix-and-chamber-length-induction]] (1)).

[F6] The dual action is $(w\cdot f)(v)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$, and $f\in wC^\circ$ if and only if $f(\rho(w)e_s)>0$ and $f(\rho(w)e_t)>0$; for every $w\in W$ and $r\in\{s,t\}$ one has $wC^\circ\subseteq rB_r$ if and only if $\ell(rw)<\ell(w)$. If $m<\infty$, the $2m$ chambers $wC^\circ$ $(w\in W)$ are exactly the $2m$ sectors cut out by the $m$ root hyperplanes $H_\beta$ $(\beta\in\Phi)$, with pairwise disjoint interiors; the corresponding closed sectors cover $V^*$, while the open sectors cover its complement of the root lines. If $m=\infty$, the chambers have pairwise disjoint interiors, the corresponding closed chambers have union $\{f\in V^*:f(e_s+e_t)>0\}\cup\{0\}$, distinct chambers are separated by a root hyperplane, and the traces $H_\beta\cap\{f:f(e_s)+f(e_t)=1\}$ are exactly the integers in the coordinate $y_s=f(e_s)$ on that affine line ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]], [[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]] (3), [[lem-cg-rank-two-prefix-and-chamber-length-induction]] (1), (4)).

proof_uses.text: 1.2 **The case $I_2(5)$: the chambers.** By [F6] the ten chambers $u_kC^\circ$ $(0\le k<10)$ are exactly the ten sectors cut out by the five root lines. By [F5], $(st)^5=1$ together with $s^2=t^2=1$ gives $su_k=u_{1-k}$ and $tu_k=u_{-1-k}$ with indices modulo $10$; combined with $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,10-k)$ this gives $\ell(su_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $1\le k\le5$, and $\ell(tu_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $5\le k\le9$. By the shortening equivalence of [F6], the chambers on the negative side of $H_{e_s}$ are exactly $u_1C^\circ,\dots,u_5C^\circ$ and those on the negative side of $H_{e_t}$ exactly $u_5C^\circ,\dots,u_9C^\circ$. [F5, F6, algebra]

1.3 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the invariant functional direction.** Here $c=1$, so $B(u,u)=B(e_s,e_s)+2B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=1-2+1=0$, $B(u,e_s)=B(e_s,e_s)+B(e_t,e_s)=1-1=0$ and $B(u,e_t)=B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=-1+1=0$, where $u:=e_s+e_t$; by bilinearity $B(u,\cdot)=0$ on $\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$. Moreover $\rho(s)u=\rho(s)e_s+\rho(s)e_t=-e_s+(e_t+2e_s)=u$ and $\rho(t)u=(e_s+2e_t)-e_t=u$, so $\rho(w)u=u$ for every $w\in W$, because $W$ is generated by $s,t$ and $\rho$ is a homomorphism. [F1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.1 **The case $A_2$: the positive roots.** By 1.1, the three vectors $e_s=\rho(1)e_s$, $e_t=\rho(1)e_t$ and $e_s+e_t=\rho(t)e_s$ are roots; they lie in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$, hence in $\Phi_+$, and they are pairwise distinct as functions on $\{s,t\}$, with values $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$. By [F6] the six chambers are cut out by the three root hyperplanes $H_\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$; the map $\alpha\mapsto H_\alpha$ from $\Phi_+$ onto these lines is injective, because two roots on one line are proportional and both have $B$-norm one by [F2], forcing the proportionality factor to be $\pm1$, and it is surjective because every $H_\beta$ equals $H_{-\beta}$ with exactly one of $\pm\beta$ in $\Phi_+$. Hence $|\Phi_+|=3$ and $\Phi_+=\{e_s,\,e_t,\,e_s+e_t\}$. [F2, F6, step 1.1]

2.2 **The case $A_2$: the chambers.** Write $y_s:=f(e_s)$ and $y_t:=f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $f$ is described by the pair $(y_s,y_t)$. By [F6], $f\in wC^\circ$ if and only if $f(\rho(w)e_s)>0$ and $f(\rho(w)e_t)>0$. Using the products $\rho(s)e_s=-e_s$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$, $\rho(t)e_t=-e_t$, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$ from [F1] and 1.1, together with $\rho(st)e_s=e_t$, $\rho(st)e_t=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_s=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_t=e_s$, $\rho(sts)e_s=-e_t$, $\rho(sts)e_t=-e_s$ (computed from $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$), this gives $C^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_t>0\}$, $sC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$, $stC^\circ=\{y_t>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$, $stsC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_t<0\}=-C^\circ$, $tsC^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$ and $tC^\circ=\{y_t<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$. On each of these six sets the signs of $(y_s,\,y_t,\,y_s+y_t)$ are the six distinct patterns $(+,+,+)$, $(-,+,+)$, $(-,+,-)$, $(-,-,-)$, $(+,-,-)$, $(+,-,+)$; these are exactly the six combinations not excluded by one of the three equations $y_s=0$, $y_t=0$, $y_s+y_t=0$, so the six chambers are the six sectors, in the stated cyclic order. By [F5], $s^2=t^2=1$ and $(st)^3=1$ give $s(st)^j=(ts)^js$ and $t(st)^j=(ts)^jt$ for all $j\ge0$ and $(ts)^j=(st)^{-j}$, whence $su_k=u_{1-k}$ and $tu_k=u_{-1-k}$ with indices read modulo $6$; combined with $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,6-k)$ this gives $\ell(su_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\ell(tu_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$. By the shortening equivalence of [F6], $H_{e_s}$ separates $C^\circ$ from $u_1C^\circ,u_2C^\circ,u_3C^\circ$ and $H_{e_t}$ from $u_3C^\circ,u_4C^\circ,u_5C^\circ$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.5 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the inversion sets.** By [F5] the $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell(u_k)=k$, and $u_{2k}=(st)^k$, $u_{2k+1}=(st)^ks$. We prove by induction on $k\ge0$ the two formulas $N((st)^k)=\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le 2k-1\}$ and $N((st)^ks)=\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le 2k\}$. For $k=0$ the first is $N(1)=\emptyset$ and the second is $N(s)=\{e_s\}$. Assume the second formula for some $k\ge0$. Since $\ell((st)^{k+1})=2k+2>2k+1=\ell((st)^ks)$, the recursion of [F3] gives $N((st)^{k+1})=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N((st)^ks)$; by 1.3, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+2e_t=u+e_t$, so $\rho(t)\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le2k\}=\{ju+u+e_t:0\le j\le2k\}=\{(j+1)u+e_t:0\le j\le2k\}$ and therefore $N((st)^{k+1})=\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le2k+1\}$, which is the first formula with $k+1$. Since $\ell((st)^{k+1}s)=2k+3>2k+2=\ell((st)^{k+1})$, again, but with $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+2e_s=u+e_s$ from 1.3, $N((st)^{k+1}s)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)\{ju+e_t:0\le j\le2k+1\}=\{ju+e_s:0\le j\le2k+2\}$, the second formula with $k+1$. So both formulas hold for all $k\ge0$. Their elements are pairwise distinct because $u\ne0$, so the two sets have cardinalities $2k$ and $2k+1$, equal to $\ell((st)^k)=2k$ and $\ell((st)^ks)=2k+1$ by [F5], in agreement with [F4]. [F3, F4, F5, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 **The case $A_2$: the inversion sets.** By [F3] and 1.1, and since $\ell(u_0)=0<\ell(u_1)=1<\ell(u_2)=2<\ell(u_3)=3$ by [F5], one has $N(s)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(1)=\{e_s\}$, $N(t)=\{e_t\}$, $N(st)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(s)=\{e_t,\,e_s+e_t\}$, $N(ts)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(t)=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t\}$ and $N(sts)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(st)=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t,\,\rho(s)(e_s+e_t)\}=\{e_s,\,e_s+e_t,\,e_t\}=\Phi_+$, where we used $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$ and $\rho(s)(e_s+e_t)=\rho(s)e_s+\rho(s)e_t=-e_s+(e_s+e_t)=e_t$; also $N(1)=\emptyset$. The cardinalities $0,1,1,2,2,3$ equal $\ell(1),\ell(s),\ell(t),\ell(st),\ell(ts),\ell(sts)$ by [F5], as asserted. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 **The case $I_2(5)$: the positive roots.** By 2.3 and [F1], $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, and using $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$ one computes $\rho(st)e_s=\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=-e_s+\phi(e_t+\phi e_s)=(\phi^2-1)e_s+\phi e_t=\phi(e_s+e_t)$. Hence the five vectors $e_s=\rho(1)e_s$, $e_t=\rho(1)e_t$, $e_t+\phi e_s=\rho(s)e_t$, $e_s+\phi e_t=\rho(t)e_s$ and $\phi(e_s+e_t)=\rho(st)e_s$ are roots; each lies in $V_+\setminus\{0\}$, so all five lie in $\Phi_+$, and they are pairwise distinct as functions on $\{s,t\}$, with values $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(\phi,1)$, $(1,\phi)$, $(\phi,\phi)$. By [F6] the ten chambers are cut out by the five root hyperplanes $H_\beta$, $\beta\in\Phi$, and as in 2.1 the map $\alpha\mapsto H_\alpha$ is a bijection from $\Phi_+$ onto these lines, so $|\Phi_+|=5$ and the five listed vectors exhaust $\Phi_+$; each of them has $B$-norm one because it is a root, by [F2]. [F1, F2, F6, step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 **The case $I_2(5)$: the inversion sets $N(u_k)$, $1\le k\le5$.** By [F5], $\ell(u_k)=k$ for $1\le k\le5$, so each step below is a shortening-free step of the recursion of [F3] and the union is disjoint. Starting from $N(1)=\emptyset$ and using the reflection values $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$, $\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=\phi(e_s+e_t)$, $\rho(t)(e_t+\phi e_s)=\phi(e_s+e_t)$, $\rho(t)\phi(e_s+e_t)=\phi e_s+e_t$ and $\rho(s)\phi(e_s+e_t)=e_s+\phi e_t$ (all from [F1], $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$) one computes $N(u_1)=\{e_s\}$, $N(u_2)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(u_1)=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t\}$, $N(u_3)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_2)=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s,\ \phi(e_s+e_t)\}$, $N(u_4)=\{e_t\}\sqcup\rho(t)N(u_3)=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ \phi(e_s+e_t),\ e_t+\phi e_s\}$ and $N(u_5)=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_4)=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s,\ \phi(e_s+e_t),\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ e_t\}=\Phi_+$, the last equality by 3.2. This gives the displayed sets $N(u_1),\dots,N(u_5)$, of cardinalities $k=|N(u_k)|=\ell(u_k)$ as required by [F4]. [F3, F4, F5, step 3.2, algebra]

5.1 **The case $I_2(5)$: the inversion sets $N(u_k)$, $5\le k<10$.** Since $N(u_5)=\Phi_+$ by 4.1, the reflection $\rho(u_5)$ maps $\Phi_+$ bijectively onto $\Phi_-$ (as $N(u_5)=\Phi_+$ means $\rho(u_5)\Phi_+\subseteq\Phi_-$, and $\rho(u_5)$ induces a bijection of $\Phi$); hence for $\alpha\in\Phi_+$: $\alpha\in N(u_5w)$ if and only if $\rho(w)\alpha\in\Phi_+$, because $\rho(u_5)$ maps $\Phi_+$ onto $\Phi_-$ and $\Phi_-$ onto $\Phi_+$. Comparing with the definition of $N(w)$ this gives $N(u_5w)=\Phi_+\setminus N(w)$ for every $w\in W$. For $5\le k<10$ one has $u_k=u_5\,u_{k-5}'$, where $u_j'$ is the alternating word of length $j$ beginning with $t$; hence $N(u_k)=\Phi_+\setminus N(u_{k-5}')$. In particular $N(u_6)=\Phi_+\setminus\{e_t\}$ and, using the recursion of [F3] once more for $u_2'=ts$ (read with the roles of $s$ and $t$ exchanged, $\ell(u_2')=2>\ell(t)=1$), $N(u_2')=\{e_s\}\sqcup\rho(s)N(u_1')=\{e_s,\ e_t+\phi e_s\}$, so that $N(u_7)=\Phi_+\setminus N(u_2')=\{e_t,\ e_s+\phi e_t,\ \phi(e_s+e_t)\}$, of cardinality $3=\ell(u_7)$. [F3, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the chambers.** Let $\delta(f):=f(e_s)+f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $\delta(f)=f(u)$; since $\rho(w)u=u$ for all $w$ by 1.3, the value $\delta(f)$ is preserved by the dual action: $\delta(w\cdot f)=(w\cdot f)(u)=f(\rho(w)^{-1}u)=f(u)=\delta(f)$. On $L:=\{f:\delta(f)=1\}$ with coordinate $y_s=f(e_s)$, $C^\circ$ has trace $(0,1)$. By [F1] and the dual action in [F6], $s$ acts by $y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t$ by $y_s\mapsto2-y_s$; hence $st$ acts by translation $y_s\mapsto y_s-2$. It follows that $(st)^kC^\circ\cap L=(-2k,1-2k)$ and $(st)^ksC^\circ\cap L=(-2k-1,-2k)$ for every integer $k$. These are all intervals $(j,j+1)$, and all group elements are alternating words by [F5] (cancelling adjacent equal letters); therefore these are exactly the open chamber traces, and no integer point belongs to one. Every chamber is a nonempty cone contained in $\{\delta>0\}$, since this holds for $C^\circ$ and $\delta$ is invariant. Each chamber $K$ equals the cone $\{\lambda x:\lambda>0,\ x\in K\cap L\}$ over its trace, because for $f\in K$ its normalisation $f/\delta(f)$ lies in $K\cap L$ and $f=\delta(f)\,(f/\delta(f))$ with $\delta(f)>0$; hence the chambers are exactly the cones over the intervals $(j,j+1)$. Finally $H_{e_s}\cap L$ is the point with $y_s=0$, and $H_{e_t}\cap L$ is the point with $y_s=1$, because $y_t=1-y_s$ on $L$. Together with 1.1-1.3, 2.1-2.5, 3.1-3.2, 4.1 and 5.1 this verifies all the claims of (i), (ii) and (iii). [F1, F5, F6, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

changed_supplier_uses.supplier_clause_check: Statement(1),(2),(3)(i)-(iv): basis, involutivity/form-preservation/fixed hyperplane for NONISOTROPIC a; finite distinct-generator ranktwo positive plane/exact order; infinite block I+N, N^2=0, no global nondegeneracy.
citation_contexts: [F1] $B(e_s,e_s)=B(e_t,e_t)=1$ and $B(e_s,e_t)=-c$; the reflection $r_a$ with normal $a$, $B(a,a)\ne0$, is $r_a(v)=v-\frac{2B(v,a)}{B(a,a)}a$, so that $r_s(e_s)=-e_s$, $r_s(e_t)=e_t+2ce_s$ and $r_t(e_t)=-e_t$, $r_t(e_s)=e_s+2ce_t$ ([[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[lem-cg-reflection-form-invariance-and-rank-two-orders]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.1 **The case $A_2$: the constant.** Put $x:=\pi/3$, $q:=\cos x$ and $r:=\sin x$. The addition formulas give $\cos 2x=\cos^2x-\sin^2x=2q^2-1$ and $\sin 2x=2qr$, hence $\cos 3x=\cos(2x+x)=(2q^2-1)q-(2qr)r=2q^3-q-2q(1-q^2)=4q^3-3q$; since $3x=\pi$ and $\cos\pi=-1$, we get $4q^3-3q+1=0$, that is $(q+1)(2q-1)^2=0$. Now $0<\pi/3<\pi/2<\pi$ and cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos 0=1$ and $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, so $0<q<1$; hence $q\ne-1$ and $q=1/2$. Thus in this case $c=1/2$, and the reflection formulas of [F1] give $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$. [F1, F7, algebra]

1.3 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the invariant functional direction.** Here $c=1$, so $B(u,u)=B(e_s,e_s)+2B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=1-2+1=0$, $B(u,e_s)=B(e_s,e_s)+B(e_t,e_s)=1-1=0$ and $B(u,e_t)=B(e_s,e_t)+B(e_t,e_t)=-1+1=0$, where $u:=e_s+e_t$; by bilinearity $B(u,\cdot)=0$ on $\mathbb Re_s+\mathbb Re_t$. Moreover $\rho(s)u=\rho(s)e_s+\rho(s)e_t=-e_s+(e_t+2e_s)=u$ and $\rho(t)u=(e_s+2e_t)-e_t=u$, so $\rho(w)u=u$ for every $w\in W$, because $W$ is generated by $s,t$ and $\rho$ is a homomorphism. [F1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.2 **The case $A_2$: the chambers.** Write $y_s:=f(e_s)$ and $y_t:=f(e_t)$ for $f\in V^*$, so that $f$ is described by the pair $(y_s,y_t)$. By [F6], $f\in wC^\circ$ if and only if $f(\rho(w)e_s)>0$ and $f(\rho(w)e_t)>0$. Using the products $\rho(s)e_s=-e_s$, $\rho(s)e_t=e_s+e_t$, $\rho(t)e_t=-e_t$, $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+e_t$ from [F1] and 1.1, together with $\rho(st)e_s=e_t$, $\rho(st)e_t=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_s=-e_s-e_t$, $\rho(ts)e_t=e_s$, $\rho(sts)e_s=-e_t$, $\rho(sts)e_t=-e_s$ (computed from $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$), this gives $C^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_t>0\}$, $sC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$, $stC^\circ=\{y_t>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$, $stsC^\circ=\{y_s<0,\ y_t<0\}=-C^\circ$, $tsC^\circ=\{y_s>0,\ y_s+y_t<0\}$ and $tC^\circ=\{y_t<0,\ y_s+y_t>0\}$. On each of these six sets the signs of $(y_s,\,y_t,\,y_s+y_t)$ are the six distinct patterns $(+,+,+)$, $(-,+,+)$, $(-,+,-)$, $(-,-,-)$, $(+,-,-)$, $(+,-,+)$; these are exactly the six combinations not excluded by one of the three equations $y_s=0$, $y_t=0$, $y_s+y_t=0$, so the six chambers are the six sectors, in the stated cyclic order. By [F5], $s^2=t^2=1$ and $(st)^3=1$ give $s(st)^j=(ts)^js$ and $t(st)^j=(ts)^jt$ for all $j\ge0$ and $(ts)^j=(st)^{-j}$, whence $su_k=u_{1-k}$ and $tu_k=u_{-1-k}$ with indices read modulo $6$; combined with $\ell(u_k)=\min(k,6-k)$ this gives $\ell(su_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ and $\ell(tu_k)=\ell(u_k)-1$ exactly for $k\in\{3,4,5\}$. By the shortening equivalence of [F6], $H_{e_s}$ separates $C^\circ$ from $u_1C^\circ,u_2C^\circ,u_3C^\circ$ and $H_{e_t}$ from $u_3C^\circ,u_4C^\circ,u_5C^\circ$. [F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.4 **The case $I_2(\infty)$: the positive roots.** Put $\Psi:=\{e_s+ku:k\ge0\}\cup\{e_t+ku:k\ge0\}$. First, $\Psi\subseteq\Phi_+$: clearly $e_s,e_t\in\Psi\cap\Phi_+$, and for $k\ge1$ the identities $e_s+ku=\rho(s)(e_t+(k-1)u)$ and $e_t+ku=\rho(t)(e_s+(k-1)u)$ hold by 1.3, so induction on $k$ shows that every element of $\Psi$ is a root; every element of $\Psi$ has nonnegative coefficients in $e_s,e_t$, so $\Psi\subseteq\Phi\cap V_+\setminus\{0\}=\Phi_+$. Conversely, $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$ is stable under $\rho(s)$ and $\rho(t)$: by 1.3 one has $\rho(s)(e_s+ku)=-e_s+ku$, which is $e_t+(k-1)u$ for $k\ge1$ and $-e_s$ for $k=0$; $\rho(s)(e_t+ku)=(e_t+2e_s)+ku=e_s+(k+1)u$; $\rho(t)(e_t+ku)=-e_t+ku$, which is $e_s+(k-1)u$ for $k\ge1$ and $-e_t$ for $k=0$; and $\rho(t)(e_s+ku)=(e_s+2e_t)+ku=e_t+(k+1)u$. Since $W$ is generated by $s,t$ and $\rho$ is a homomorphism, $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$ is stable under every $\rho(w)$; it contains $e_s,e_t$, so it contains the orbit $\Phi$. Hence $\Phi\subseteq\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$, and an element of $\Phi_+$ lies in $\Psi$: it lies in $\Psi\cup(-\Psi)$, and no element of $-\Psi$ has all coefficients nonnegative, while the elements of $V_+$ do. Therefore $\Phi_+=\Psi$; finally the two families $e_s+ku$ and $e_t+ku$ are disjoint and each is injective in $k$, because $u\ne0$ while evaluating $e_s+ku=e_s+k'u$ at $s$ gives $k=k'$, and $e_s+ku=e_t+k'u$ would give $1+k=k'$ at $s$ and $k=1+k'$ at $t$, hence $k=k+2$, a contradiction; so $\Phi_+$ is infinite. [F1, F2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.2 **The case $I_2(5)$: the positive roots.** By 2.3 and [F1], $\rho(s)e_t=e_t+\phi e_s$ and $\rho(t)e_s=e_s+\phi e_t$, and using $\rho(uv)=\rho(u)\rho(v)$ and $\phi^2=\phi+1$ one computes $\rho(st)e_s=\rho(s)(e_s+\phi e_t)=-e_s+\phi(e_t+\phi e_s)=(\phi^2-1)e_s+\phi e_t=\phi(e_s+e_t)$. proof_uses.text: 2.1 The Gram realisation. By step 1.1 and [F1] the Cholesky factorisation $C=LL^{T}$ exists with $L$ invertible, and [F3] gives that its rows $u_0,\dots,u_3$ are unit vectors with $u_i\cdot u_j=c_{ij}$; thus $u_i\cdot u_j=\tfrac12$ for $i\ne j$, the pairwise angular distances are $\arccos\tfrac12$, and every point of $\Sigma(C)$ has unique barycentric ray coordinates. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 The hemisphere functional. Let $w:=\tfrac25(u_0+u_1+u_2+u_3)$ and $\varphi(x):=\langle w,x\rangle$. Since every row of $C$ sums to $1+3c=\tfrac52$, for each fixed $j$ one has $\langle w,u_j\rangle=\tfrac25\sum_i\langle u_i,u_j\rangle=\tfrac25\cdot\tfrac52=1$; hence $\varphi(u_i)=1$ for all $i$, so by [F3] $\varphi(\sum_i\lambda_iu_i)=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and $\varphi\equiv1$ on $\Delta(C)$. Therefore $\Sigma(C)\subseteq\{x:\varphi(x)>0\}$, the open hemisphere. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

3.2 The vertex link. By [F3] and the Schur formula with $c=\tfrac12$, the link of $u_0$ has Gram matrix $C^{\mathrm{lk}}$ whose diagonal entries are $1$ and whose off-diagonal entries are $\frac{c-c^2}{1-c^2}=\frac{1/2-1/4}{3/4}=\frac13$. Its quadratic form is $y^{T}C^{\mathrm{lk}}y=\frac23\lVert y\rVert^2+\frac13(\sum_iy_i)^2$, which is positive for $y\ne0$; so the link is the spherical triangle whose three angular distances are $\arccos\frac13$. [step 2.1, F3, algebra]

4.1 The two-step Schur value. Iterating the Schur formula of [F3] over the vertices $u_0,u_1$ means applying it first to the Gram matrix of the link of $u_0$, whose off-diagonal entries are $\frac13$ by step 3.2, and then to a $2\times2$ block; the resulting off-diagonal entry is $\frac{1/3-(1/3)^2}{1-(1/3)^2}=\frac{2/9}{8/9}=\frac14$, the same value as the projected cosine of step 3.3. [step 3.2, step 3.3, F3, algebra]

5.1 Order independence and conclusion. By [F3] the link of the face spanned by $u_0,u_1$ equals the Gram matrix of the normalised orthogonal projections of the remaining vertices onto $\operatorname{span}(u_0,u_1)^\perp$, so the projection computation of step 3.3 and the iterated Schur computation of step 4.1 are two descriptions of the same matrix; they agree at the value $\tfrac14$, the face link is an arc of angular length $\arccos\tfrac14$, and the positivity check is the one of step 3.2 applied to this $2\times2$ block, whose determinant $1-\tfrac1{16}$ is positive. [step 3.3, step 4.1, F3] ∎

citation_contexts: Let $L$ be a finite lattice, let $\theta$ be a lattice congruence on $L$ ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]) and let $[x]_\theta$ be the class of $x\in L$. Then:

[F1] $\theta$ is a lattice congruence: $x\equiv_\theta x'$ and $y\equiv_\theta y'$ imply $x\wedge y\equiv_\theta x'\wedge y'$ and $x\vee y\equiv_\theta x'\vee y'$ ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.1 Assume $x\equiv_\theta y$. Apply [F1] to the pairs $(x\equiv_\theta y,\;y\equiv_\theta y)$, the second entry being licensed by reflexivity in [F3]: this gives $x\wedge y\equiv_\theta y\wedge y$ and $x\vee y\equiv_\theta y\vee y$. By [F2] with antisymmetry, $y\wedge y=y=y\vee y$, so $x\wedge y\equiv_\theta y$ and $x\vee y\equiv_\theta y$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.3 Assume $x\equiv_\theta x'$ and $y\equiv_\theta y'$. By [F1], $x\vee y\equiv_\theta x'\vee y'$ and $x\wedge y\equiv_\theta x'\wedge y'$, so $[x\vee y]_\theta=[x'\vee y']_\theta$ and $[x\wedge y]_\theta=[x'\wedge y']_\theta$ by [F3]. Hence the proposed operations $[x]_\theta\vee[y]_\theta:=[x\vee y]_\theta$ and $[x]_\theta\wedge[y]_\theta:=[x\wedge y]_\theta$ do not depend on the chosen representatives, and the class of $x$, hence the proposed pair of endpoints of its class, depends only on $[x]_\theta$. [F1, F3]

4.3 Let $z\in L$. If $z\in C$ then $\pi_\downarrow(x)\le z\le\pi_\uparrow(x)$, since these are the least and the greatest member of $C$. Conversely assume $\pi_\downarrow(x)\le z\le\pi_\uparrow(x)$ and put $a:=\pi_\downarrow(x)$, $b:=\pi_\uparrow(x)$; both lie in $C$, so $a\equiv_\theta b$ by [F3]. Apply [F1] to the pairs $a\equiv_\theta b$ and $z\equiv_\theta z$: $a\wedge z\equiv_\theta b\wedge z$. Since $a\le z$ we have $a\wedge z=a$ by [F2], and since $z\le b$ we have $b\wedge z=z$ by [F2]; hence $a\equiv_\theta z$, so $z\in C$ by [F3]. Therefore $[x]_\theta=\{z\in L:\pi_\downarrow(x)\le z\le\pi_\uparrow(x)\}$, the asserted interval identity. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.2]

4.4 Monotonicity of the upper endpoint map. Assume $x\le y$. By [F3], $\pi_\uparrow(x)\equiv_\theta x$ and $\pi_\uparrow(y)\equiv_\theta y$, so [F1] gives $\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)\equiv_\theta x\vee y=y\equiv_\theta\pi_\uparrow(y)$; thus $\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)$ lies in the class of $y$, whose greatest member is $\pi_\uparrow(y)$, so $\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)\le\pi_\uparrow(y)$. With $\pi_\uparrow(y)\le\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)$ from [F2], antisymmetry gives $\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)=\pi_\uparrow(y)$, and then $\pi_\uparrow(x)\le\pi_\uparrow(x)\vee\pi_\uparrow(y)=\pi_\uparrow(y)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.2]

4.5 Monotonicity of the lower endpoint map. Assume $x\le y$. By [F3], $\pi_\downarrow(x)\equiv_\theta x$ and $\pi_\downarrow(y)\equiv_\theta y$, so [F1] gives $\pi_\downarrow(x)\wedge\pi_\downarrow(y)\equiv_\theta x\wedge y=x\equiv_\theta\pi_\downarrow(x)$; thus $\pi_\downarrow(x)\wedge\pi_\downarrow(y)$ lies in the class of $x$, whose least member is $\pi_\downarrow(x)$, so $\pi_\downarrow(x)\le\pi_\downarrow(x)\wedge\pi_\downarrow(y)$. With $\pi_\downarrow(x)\wedge\pi_\downarrow(y)\le\pi_\downarrow(x)$ from [F2], antisymmetry gives equality, and then $\pi_\downarrow(x)=\pi_\downarrow(x)\wedge\pi_\downarrow(y)\le\pi_\downarrow(y)$ by [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, step 3.2]

citation_contexts: Let $P$ be a finite graded poset, let $x\le y$ in $P$, and let $[x,y]$ carry a descending rooted-chain labeling with values in a linearly ordered set that satisfies the no-tie condition (N) and the lex-increasing property (L) on every rooted interval ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]). Write $n:=\rho(x,y)$; for a maximal chain $m$ of $[x,y]$ write $\lambda(m)$ for its label word and $D(m)\subseteq\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ for its descent set, and identify $m$ with its vertex set, so that $|m|=n+1$.

[F2] Maximal chains of $[x,y]$ are the chains $y=m_0\gtrdot m_1\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_n=x$ with $n=\rho(x,y)$, equivalently the chains of $[x,y]$ contained in no larger chain of $[x,y]$; $|m|=n+1$ for each, and the label word of $m$ is $\lambda(m)=(\lambda_1(m),\dots,\lambda_n(m))$ with $\lambda_i(m):=\lambda(m_0\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_{i-1};\,m_i\lessdot m_{i-1})$. In the rooted interval $([v,w],c)$ the root chain stays fixed, and a maximal chain $v=w_0\lessdot w_1\lessdot\cdots\lessdot w_k=w$ of $[v,w]$ has label word with $i$-th entry $\lambda(c+w_{k-1}\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot w_{k-i+1};\,w_{k-i}\lessdot w_{k-i+1})$: the word of a maximal chain of $[x,y]$ restricted to a rooted subinterval is exactly the corresponding block of its label word ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]).

[F3] No-tie (N): in every rooted interval the labels of any maximal chain are pairwise distinct. Lex-increasing (L): in every rooted interval there is exactly one increasing maximal chain, and its label word is lexicographically first among the label words of all maximal chains of that rooted interval ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]).

[F4] The descent set is $D(m)=\{i:\lambda_i(m)>\lambda_{i+1}(m)\}$, so $m$ is strictly falling if and only if $D(m)=\{1,\dots,n-1\}$; the word of $m$ is falling when $\lambda_1(m)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n(m)$, and under (N) falling and strictly falling agree on each maximal chain; words are compared lexicographically ([[def-cg-finite-lattice-congruence-and-interval-projections]]).

proof_uses.text: 2.1 Replacement chain of (i). Put $c':=m_0\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_{e-1}$. The segment $m_{e-1}\gtrdot m_e\gtrdot m_{e+1}$ is a maximal chain of the rooted interval $([m_{e+1},m_{e-1}],c')$, and by [F2] its word there is $(\lambda_e(m),\lambda_{e+1}(m))$, which is falling by step 1.3, hence not increasing. By (L) of [F3] this rooted interval has exactly one increasing maximal chain; it is not the segment, so it has the form $m_{e-1}\gtrdot y'\gtrdot m_{e+1}$ with $m_{e+1}<y'<m_{e-1}$ and $y'\ne m_e$, and its word $(a,b)$ satisfies $a<b$ and $(a,b)\prec(\lambda_e(m),\lambda_{e+1}(m))$ because it is lexicographically first. Define $k:=m_0\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_{e-1}\gtrdot y'\gtrdot m_{e+1}\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_n$. [F2, F3, step 1.3]

2.2 Setup of (ii). Fix a rooted interval $([v,w],c)$ of $[x,y]$ and put $k:=\rho(v,w)$; we treat $k\ge1$ and return to $k=0$ below. For a subset $S$ of $\{1,\dots,k-1\}$ write $k-S:=\{k-s:s\in S\}$. For $T\subseteq\{1,\dots,k-1\}$ let $f(T)$ be the number of maximal chains $m$ of $[v,w]$ (maximal in the poset $[v,w]$, carrying the labeling induced by the root chain $c$ as in [F2]) with $D(m)\subseteq T$, and for $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,k-1\}$ let $\alpha(S)$ be the number of strict chains $w=y_0>y_1>\cdots>y_t=v$ with $t\ge1$ whose rank set $\{\rho(y_i)-\rho(v):1\le i\le t-1\}$ equals $S$. Both are finite counts by [F9], and by step 1.1 the rank set of each such chain is a subset of $\{1,\dots,k-1\}$. [F2, F4, F9, step 1.1]

3.1 Refinement construction. Given a strict chain $w=y_0>y_1>\cdots>y_t=v$ with rank set $S$, construct a maximal chain $m$ of $[v,w]$ top-down: starting from the top segment $[y_1,y_0]$ and continuing downwards, replace the segment $[y_i,y_{i-1}]$ by the unique increasing maximal chain of the rooted interval $([y_i,y_{i-1}],c_i)$, where $c_i$ is the original root $c$ extended by the part already constructed from $w$ down to $y_{i-1}$, so it ends at the upper endpoint $y_{i-1}$ (and $c_1=c$). Each replacement exists and is unique by (L) of [F3], and the resulting chain is a maximal chain of $[v,w]$. Inside each segment the word is increasing, so a descent of $\lambda(m)$ can occur only at a junction $y_i$, $1\le i\le t-1$, whose word position is $k-(\rho(y_i)-\rho(v))\in k-S$; hence $D(m)\subseteq k-S$. [F2, F3, step 2.2]

3.2 Verification of the replacement. By [F2] the chain $k$ of step 2.1 is a maximal chain of $[x,y]$: it has length $n$, and each of its steps is a cover of $P$. Its word agrees with $\lambda(m)$ in positions $1,\dots,e-1$ because $k$ and $m$ share the chain $m_0\gtrdot\cdots\gtrdot m_{e-1}$ and the covers among these vertices, while at positions $e$ and $e+1$ the entries are $(a,b)$ and $(\lambda_e(m),\lambda_{e+1}(m))$ with $(a,b)\prec(\lambda_e(m),\lambda_{e+1}(m))$; hence $\lambda(k)\prec\lambda(m)$. Moreover $k\cap m=m\setminus\{m_e\}$: the only vertex of $m$ strictly between $m_{e+1}$ and $m_{e-1}$ is $m_e$ and $y'\ne m_e$, while every other vertex of $m$ lies outside that open interval, so $|k\cap m|=|m|-1$; and since $d<e<g$, step 1.3 gives $m'\cap m\subseteq\{m_i:i\le d\text{ or }i\ge g\}\subseteq m\setminus\{m_e\}=k\cap m$. [F2, step 1.3, step 2.1]

4.1 Truncation construction and the count. Conversely, given a maximal chain $m$ of $[v,w]$ with $D(m)\subseteq k-S$, keep the elements $m_j$ with $k-j\in S$; these are exactly $|S|$ indices in $\{1,\dots,k-1\}$, and together with the endpoints $w=m_0$ and $v=m_k$ they form a strict chain of $|S|+1$ steps whose rank set is $S$. Between two consecutive kept elements there is no descent of $D(m)$: a junction $m_i$ strictly between two consecutive kept elements has $k-i
otin S$, hence $i
otin k-S$, and $D(m)\subseteq k-S$ gives $i
otin D(m)$; so the word of each segment is weakly increasing, hence strictly increasing by (N), hence the segment is the unique increasing chain of its rooted interval by (L), so refining the kept chain returns $m$. Thus the constructions of step 3.1 and of this step are mutually inverse bijections, and $\alpha(S)=f(k-S)$ for every $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,k-1\}$. [F2, F3, step 3.1]

4.2 Facets and the open interval. Interpreting the maximal chains as facets of the order complex by [F5], step 3.2 says that for facets $C_{m'}$ preceding $C_m$ in the lexicographic order of label words there is a facet $C_k$ with $C_{m'}\cap C_m\subseteq C_k\cap C_m$ and $|C_k\cap C_m|=|C_m|-1$, and $\lambda(k)\prec\lambda(m)$ so that $C_k$ precedes $C_m$; this is the pairwise facet criterion of the statement. Indeed, every face of $C_m$ shared with an earlier facet lies in an earlier intersection obtained by deleting one vertex from $C_m$. Distinct facets have the same cardinality by [F2], so no earlier intersection is larger; hence the intersection of the simplex on $C_m$ with the union of earlier facet simplices is pure of codimension one, which is the shelling condition. A chain of the open interval $(x,y)$ is contained in no larger chain of $(x,y)$ precisely when, after adjoining $x$ and $y$, it becomes a maximal chain of $[x,y]$: if it could be enlarged inside $(x,y)$, so could the enlarged chain in $[x,y]$, and conversely an enlargement in $[x,y]$ of a chain already containing $x$ and $y$ lies in $(x,y)$. Hence the facets of $\Delta((x,y))$ are the sets $m\setminus\{x,y\}$ for maximal chains $m$ of $[x,y]$, and since $x,y\in C_k\cap C_m$, deleting $x,y$ from all facets preserves $C_{m'}\cap C_m\subseteq C_k\cap C_m$ and gives $|(C_k\cap C_m)\setminus\{x,y\}|=|C_m\setminus\{x,y\}|-1$. For $n=0$ or $n=1$ there is only one maximal chain and one open-interval facet, the empty face, so the shelling condition is vacuous. [F2, F5, step 3.2]

4.3 Tied words. Suppose instead that $\lambda(m')=\lambda(m)$ with $m'\ne m$. The analysis of step 1.3 applies verbatim with the single change that the window words of $m$ and $m'$ coincide; that common window is again not increasing, since if it were increasing both window subchains would be increasing maximal chains of the same rooted interval and, being distinct because $m_i\ne m'_i$ for $d<i<g$, would contradict the uniqueness in (L). So there is again a descent $\lambda_e(m)>\lambda_{e+1}(m)$ at some $e\in\{d+1,\dots,g-1\}$, and steps 2.1 and 3.2 produce a maximal chain $k$ with $\lambda(k)\prec\lambda(m)=\lambda(m')$, $|k\cap m|=|m|-1$ and $m'\cap m\subseteq k\cap m$. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.2]

6.1 Evaluation and the formula in rank $k\ge1$. By step 2.2 and 1.1, each strict chain with $t$ steps contributes to $\alpha(S)$ with $|S|=t-1$, so the alternating sum of step 5.1 equals $\sum_{t\ge1}(-1)^{k-t}c_t(v,w)=(-1)^k\sum_{t\ge1}(-1)^tc_t(v,w)=(-1)^k\mu(v,w)$ by the chain-sum identity of step 1.2; hence the number of maximal chains with $D(m)=\{1,\dots,k-1\}$, that is, of strictly falling maximal chains by [F4], equals $(-1)^k\mu(v,w)$, which is the stated formula $\mu(v,w)=(-1)^{\rho(v,w)}\cdot\#\{$strictly falling maximal chains$\}$ since $k=\rho(v,w)$. For $k=0$ we have $v=w$; then $\mu(v,v)=1$ by [F6] and the single rank-$0$ maximal chain has an empty label word and is vacuously falling, so the formula holds as well. [F4, F6, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 5.1]

7.1 Both parts are proved. Part (i) is steps 4.2, 4.3 and 5.2, and part (ii) is steps 1.2 and 6.1 together with step 2.2 for the definition of the counted chains: since the rooted interval $([v,w],c)$ was arbitrary, the formula holds for every one of them, with $k=\rho(v,w)$; under (N) falling and strictly falling agree on each maximal chain by [F4], so 'falling' may replace 'strictly falling'; and the conventions $\mu(v,v)=1$ with the singleton maximal chain having an empty label word and being vacuously falling, and $\rho(v,w)=1$ with the open interval $(v,w)$ empty and the single maximal chain with one-term label word vacuously falling, are the rank-zero and rank-one cases of the formula. All counts are finite by [F9] and the argument uses no choice principle: the unique increasing chains and the single Boolean inversion are determined data, not selected from families. [F4, F9, step 1.2, step 6.1, step 5.2] ∎

citation_contexts: Let $X$ be an isometric polyhedral gluing with standing hypotheses (H1)-(H3) of [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], with chain metric candidate $d$, maximal dimension $D$ and finite model list. Write $P^{*}:=P\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ and let $K$ be the order complex ([[def-face-poset-and-order-complex]]) of $P^{*}$: its vertices are the elements of $P^{*}$ and its simplices are the finite chains in $P^{*}$.

[F6] The chain length of a chain is the sum of the Euclidean distances of its steps computed in any common cells, $d$ is the infimum of chain lengths, (H1)-(H3) hold, and $D$ is the maximum of the dimensions of the cells. [[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]

proof_uses.text: 3.1 The family of all convex hulls $\operatorname{conv}(b_{F_0},\dots,b_{F_k})$ over strict chains $F_0>\dots>F_k$ in $P^{*}$ is a well-defined family of subsets of $X$, the map $\Phi\colon|K|\to X$ that is affine on each simplex of $K$ with the corresponding vertex values is well defined, and it is a bijection. Each such hull lies in the cell $C_{F_0}$ and is computed there; if the same chain is regarded inside a larger cell the hull is unchanged because all its points lie in the face $C_{F_0}$ and that face is convex, so the subset of $X$ is unambiguous. The images of the simplices of $K$ are exactly the simplices of the triangulations of the cells of [step 2.1], so they cover $X$, and distinct ones have disjoint relative interiors: within one cell this is the triangulation property of [step 2.1]; and if $x$ lies in the relative interior of simplices with top faces $F$ and $G$, then $x\in\operatorname{relint}F\cap\operatorname{relint}G$ by the coning description of [step 2.1], while $x\in C_F\cap C_G=C_{F\wedge G}$ by the intersection condition of [F6]; as $C_{F\wedge G}$ is a face of $C_F$ containing $x$ and $x$ is relatively interior in $F$, that face must be $F$ itself, and likewise $G\subseteq C_{F\wedge G}$, so $F$ and $G$ are faces of one cell with a common relative interior point and hence coincide by [F2]; then the two simplices are two cells of one triangulation with a common relative interior point and hence coincide. Therefore every point of $X$ is in the relative interior of exactly one of the simplices, so $\Phi$ is bijective, and its carrier is unique. [F5, F6, step 2.1]

3.2 There is a real $L$ with $1\le L<\infty$, depending only on the finite model list, such that for every simplex of $K$ and every vertex $v$ the function $\lambda_v$ restricted to that simplex is $L$-Lipschitz for the Euclidean metric of its image. On a singleton simplex all coordinates are constant, with slope $0$. On a positive-dimensional simplex of $K$ with chain $F_0>\dots>F_k$ the function $\lambda_v$ either vanishes identically, when $v$ is not one of the $F_i$, or equals the barycentric coordinate at $b_v$; its linear part has norm $1/h$, where $h>0$ is the distance from $b_v$ to the affine hull of the remaining barycentres, because its gradient is perpendicular to that affine hull and the coordinate changes from $0$ there to $1$ over the perpendicular displacement of length $h$. Each such configuration is isometric to a configuration in a model cell, because the cells of $X$ fall into finitely many isometry classes and the face isometries are affine and isometric, so the positive-dimensional model simplices supply only finitely many positive numbers $h$. Take $L$ to be the maximum of $1$ and their reciprocals; when no such simplex exists take $L=1$. This bounds every coordinate slope. [F3, F5, F6, step 2.1]

4.2 Every point of $X$ lies in the relative interior of exactly one simplex of $K$, its carrier, of dimension at most $D$. Uniqueness and existence are [step 3.1]. A simplex of $K$ is a strict chain $F_0>\dots>F_k$ of nonempty faces; passing from $F_{i+1}$ to $F_i$ is passing to a proper face, which by [F2] lies in a supporting hyperplane, so the dimensions strictly increase along the chain: $k\le\dim F_0\le D$; the simplex therefore has $k+1\le D+1$ vertices and dimension at most $D$. [F2, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 For all $x,y\in X$ and every vertex $v$ one has $|\lambda_v(x)-\lambda_v(y)|\le L\,d(x,y)$. Let $x=x_0,\dots,x_m=y$ be a chain as in [F6]; each consecutive pair lies in a common cell, so [step 4.4] gives $|\lambda_v(x_{i-1})-\lambda_v(x_i)|\le L\,d_{p_i}(x_{i-1},x_i)$, and summing the at most $m$ inequalities and using the triangle inequality for real numbers gives $|\lambda_v(x)-\lambda_v(y)|\le L\,\ell(x_0,\dots,x_m)$. Taking the infimum over all chains from $x$ to $y$ gives the claim, since $L>0$. [F6, step 4.4, algebra]

7.1 For every vertex $v$ the closed star of $v$ is compact and metrizable, and its open star is open and hence a neighbourhood of each of its own points. The closed star is $\Phi(|S|)$ where $S$ is the subcomplex of $K$ consisting of every simplex containing $v$ together with all its faces: the simplices containing $v$ are chains in $P^{*}$ containing $v$, and the elements of $P^{*}$ comparable with $v$ are finitely many, because $P_{\le v}$ is finite by the shape condition of [F6] and the faces $q\ge v$ are finitely many by (H2) of [F6] (a cell $C_q$ meets the relative interior of $C_v$ exactly when $v\le q$). There are finitely many such chains, and each has finitely many faces, so $S$ is a finite subcomplex, $|S|$ is compact and metrizable by [F4], and its image under the homeomorphism of [step 4.1] is compact and metrizable. The open star is the union of the relative interiors of precisely the simplices containing $v$, not of all faces in $S$. Equivalently it is $\{x:\lambda_v(x)>0\}$, which is open: on each cell the coordinate is continuous by step 4.4, or for the chain metric it is Lipschitz by step 5.1. It is contained in the closed star and is a neighbourhood of each of its own points; and every $x\in X$ lies in the relative interior of its carrier, which has at least one vertex, so the open stars cover $X$. Finally, if a vertex $w$ lies in a common cell with $v$, then $w\le q$ for some $q\ge v$; there are finitely many such $q$ as just shown and each $P_{\le q}$ is finite, so only finitely many such $w$ exist. [F4, F6, F7, step 4.1, step 4.4, step 5.1] ∎

Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix on $S$, $W$ the group presented by $(S,m)$ with length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$, $B$ the Coxeter form, $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ the canonical reflection homomorphism with root system $\Phi$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual with its dual action, its chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$ and its root hyperplanes $H_\alpha$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]). For $s\in S$ put
$$B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\};$$
then $C^\circ=\bigcap_{s\in S}B_s$ and the translate $sB_s=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)<0\}$ is the opposite open half-space. For distinct $s,t$ let $W_{s,t}:=\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ be the standard parabolic subgroup, with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$, which agrees with $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2)). For $s\ne t$ and $k\ge0$ let $u_k$ be the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters beginning with $s$, so $u_0=1$.

[F2] The assignment $s\mapsto r_s$ induces the group homomorphism $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$, the root system is $\Phi=\{\rho(w)e_s:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$, every root satisfies $B(\alpha,\alpha)=1$, and $\rho(wsw^{-1})=r_{\rho(w)e_s}$ for all $w\in W$, $s\in S$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[lem-cg-reflection-representation-descends-and-root-norms]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.3 **Sectors avoid the walls.** By [F4] the interiors of the chambers $wC_P$ $(w\in W_{s,t})$ are convex open cones that are connected components of the complement of the union of the root lines in $P^*$ (respectively in $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)>0\}$ when $m(s,t)=\infty$), so each is disjoint from every root line $H_\beta\cap P^*$ $(\beta\in\Phi_P)$, and $H_{e_s}\cap P^*$, $H_{e_t}\cap P^*$ are root lines because $e_s,e_t\in\Phi_P$. An open convex set disjoint from a line lies in exactly one of the two open half-planes bounded by it. Hence for every $v\in W_{s,t}$ and $s'\in\{s,t\}$ exactly one of $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$ and $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$ holds. [F4, F2, algebra]

Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix on $S$, $W$ the group presented by $(S,m)$ with length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$, $B$ the Coxeter form, $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ the canonical reflection homomorphism with root system $\Phi$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual with its dual action, its chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$ and its root hyperplanes $H_\alpha$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]). For $s\in S$ put
$$B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\};$$
then $C^\circ=\bigcap_{s\in S}B_s$ and the translate $sB_s=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)<0\}$ is the opposite open half-space. For distinct $s,t$ let $W_{s,t}:=\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ be the standard parabolic subgroup, with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$, which agrees with $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2)). For $s\ne t$ and $k\ge0$ let $u_k$ be the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters beginning with $s$, so $u_0=1$.

[F3] The formula $(w\cdot f)(v):=f(\rho(w)^{-1}v)$ defines a left action of $W$ on $V^*$ by linear maps, $C^\circ=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)>0\text{ for all }r\in S\}$ is nonempty, and $H_\alpha=\{f\in V^*:f(\alpha)=0\}$. For $s\ne t$, in the coordinates $(y_s,y_t)$ of $P^*=\mathbb Rf_s+\mathbb Rf_t$ with dual basis $f_s(e_t)=\delta_{st}$, the dual generators act by $(y_s,y_t)\mapsto(-y_s,\ 2cy_s+y_t)$ for $s$ and $(y_s,y_t)\mapsto(y_s+2cy_t,\ -y_t)$ for $t$, each fixing the line $H_{e_s}\cap P^*$ respectively $H_{e_t}\cap P^*$ pointwise; when $m(s,t)=\infty$ the functional $f\mapsto f(e_s+e_t)$ is $W_{s,t}$-invariant ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]], [[lem-cg-dual-action-and-chamber-faces-exist]]).

proof_uses.text: 1.1 **Set-up.** For the rank-two calculation fix $s\ne t$ in $S$ and adopt the notation of [F1] and [F3]. For $r\in S$ the sets $B_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)>0\}$ and $rB_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)<0\}$ are disjoint and $C^\circ=\bigcap_{r\in S}B_r$; the dual action satisfies $v(B_s\cap B_t)=\{v\cdot f:f\in B_s\cap B_t\}$, and the action of $v\in W_{s,t}$ on $V^*$ is linear. By [F5] the intrinsic length satisfies $\ell_{s,t}(x)=\ell(x)$ for $x\in W_{s,t}$. [F1, F3, F5, given]

1.2 **Reduction to the rank-two plane.** Put $C_P^\circ:=\{g\in P^*:g(e_s)>0,\ g(e_t)>0\}$ and let $\pi:V^*\to P^*$, $\pi(f):=f|_P$. Then $\pi$ is linear and surjective, because a functional prescribed on $P$ extends to a functional on $V$ by $0$ on the remaining basis vectors. Every $v\in W_{s,t}$ preserves $P$ and fixes $P^\perp$ pointwise by [F1], so for $x\in P$ and $f\in V^*$ one has $(v\cdot f)(x)=f(\rho(v)^{-1}x)$ with $\rho(v)^{-1}x\in P$; hence $\pi(v\cdot f)=v\cdot\pi(f)$ and $\pi^{-1}(C_P^\circ)=B_s\cap B_t$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}=B_{s'}$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}=s'B_{s'}$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Consequently $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$, and $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq s'B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.5 **The infinite dihedral group.** Assume $m(s,t)=\infty$, write $u:=st$, and let $u'_k$ be the alternating word of length $k$ beginning with $t$. By [F5], $u$ has infinite order, and by [F6] $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k=\ell_{s,t}(u'_k)$ for all $k\ge0$. The union $X:=\{u_k:k\ge0\}\cup\{u'_k:k\ge0\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$ ($u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$, $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$, $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$, $u_0t=u'_1$, $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$, symmetrically for $u'_k$), so $X=W_{s,t}$; by [F6] the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k$ for every $k\ge0$, and likewise the $u'_k$. The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$. On the affine line $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$, parametrized by $y_s$, the generators act by $s:y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t:y_s\mapsto 2-y_s$ by [F3] (here $c=1$); consequently the affine map of $u_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s-2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s-2j$ for $k=2j+1$, and that of $u'_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s+2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s+2j+2$ for $k=2j+1$, by induction on $k$ (each step composes with $s$ or $t$ alternately). Hence the trace of $u_kC_P^\circ$ is the interval $(-k,-k+1)$ and that of $u'_kC_P^\circ$ is $(k,k+1)$. Since these intervals are pairwise distinct, an element of $W_{s,t}=X$ is determined by the trace of its chamber. Writing $v_j$ $(j\in\mathbb Z)$ for the element with trace $(j,j+1)$, namely $v_j=u_{-j}$ for $j\le0$ and $v_j=u'_j$ for $j\ge0$, one therefore has $\ell_{s,t}(v_j)=|j|$ together with $s\cdot v_j=v_{-j-1}$ and $t\cdot v_j=v_{1-j}$, because the affine maps send the interval $(j,j+1)$ to $(-j-1,-j)$, respectively $(1-j,2-j)$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

1.6 **Signs in the infinite case.** In the situation of 1.5 the sign of $y_s$ on $v_jC_P^\circ$ is the sign of $y_s$ on the interval $(j,j+1)$, hence negative exactly when $j\le-1$, and the sign of $y_t=1-y_s$ is negative exactly when $j\ge1$. [F3, algebra]

1.7 **(P_0) and (Q_0).** For $w=1$ one has $\ell(w)=0$, $wC^\circ=C^\circ\subseteq B_r$ for every $r\in S$ by 1.1, and choosing $u=1$ gives $C^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$ and $\ell(1)=0=\ell_{s,t}(1)+\ell(1)$ for all $s\ne t$. [F3, given]

2.1 **Signs of the finite sectors.** In the finite case let $C_k:=u_kC_P^\circ$ $(0\le k<2m)$; by [F4] these are the interiors of all $2m$ sectors. Consecutive $u_k$ differ by right multiplication by a generator $r$, so $u_kC_P$ and $u_krC_P$ share the image under $u_k$ of the wall of $C_P$ fixed by $r$ and lie on its opposite sides, by [F3]. They are adjacent sectors. The distinct vertices of the Cayley cycle in 1.4 therefore list the sectors in cyclic order. The sign of $y_s$ is constant on each $C_k$ (no $C_k$ meets the line $y_s=0$ by 1.3), is $+$ on $C_0$, and is $-$ on $C_1=sC_P^\circ$ because $s$ negates $y_s$ by [F3]. It changes exactly at those transitions whose common boundary ray lies on the line $y_s=0$: that line contains exactly two boundary rays of the arrangement, hence exactly two transitions; and the involution $s$ maps each sector to the sector on the opposite side of $y_s=0$ and fixes no sector, because $s$ swaps the two half-planes and no sector meets the wall. Hence exactly $m$ sectors lie on each side, and the negative side is the contiguous block of $m$ sectors containing $C_1$ but not $C_0$, that is $\{k:y_s<0\text{ on }C_k\}=\{1,\dots,m\}$. Applying the same argument to $t$, which is $u_{2m-1}$ and negates $y_t$, gives $\{k:y_t<0\text{ on }C_k\}=\{m,\dots,2m-1\}$. [F3, F4, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

5.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm P)$.** Fix $n\ge0$ and suppose only $(\mathrm Q_n)$. If $S$ is empty there is no $s$ to check. If $S=\{s\}$ then $W=\{1,s\}$ by $s^2=1$ and [F5], and the only positive-length chamber is $sC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$, with $\ell(s)=1$, proving $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$ directly. Now suppose $|S|\ge2$. First $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and (1) imply $(\mathrm P_n)$: for any $a$ of length $n$ and generator $r$, choose $q\ne r$ and use $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to write $a=ud$, with $aC^\circ\subseteq u(B_r\cap B_q)$ and $n=\ell_{r,q}(u)+\ell(d)$. The rank-two dichotomy gives the positive alternative or the negative alternative with $\ell_{r,q}(ru)=\ell_{r,q}(u)-1$; in the latter case $\ell(ra)\le\ell_{r,q}(ru)+\ell(d)=n-1$, hence equality by [F5]. This is $(\mathrm P_n)$. Let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and let $s\in S$; choose $t$ with $w=tw'$ and $\ell(w')=n$. If $s=t$, then $(\mathrm P_n)$ applied to $w'$ gives $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$: the second alternative would give $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=n-1$, whereas $\ell(sw')=\ell(w)=n+1$ here. Hence $wC^\circ=t(w'C^\circ)\subseteq tB_s=sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(w')=n=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. If $s\ne t$, apply $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to $w'$: there is $u\in W_{s,t}$ with $w'C^\circ\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w')=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w')$. Put $v:=tu\in W_{s,t}$. If $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$, then $wC^\circ\subseteq tu(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$. Let $S$ be a finite set, $m$ a Coxeter matrix on $S$, $W$ the group presented by $(S,m)$ with length function $\ell$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]), $V=\mathbb R^S$, $B$ the Coxeter form, $\rho:W\to\mathrm{GL}(V)$ the canonical reflection homomorphism with root system $\Phi$ ([[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]]), and let $V^*$ be the algebraic dual with its dual action, its chamber $C$, its interior $C^\circ$ and its root hyperplanes $H_\alpha$ ([[def-cg-dual-chambers-and-reflection-hyperplanes]]). For $s\in S$ put
$$B_s:=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)>0\};$$
then $C^\circ=\bigcap_{s\in S}B_s$ and the translate $sB_s=\{f\in V^*:f(e_s)<0\}$ is the opposite open half-space. For distinct $s,t$ let $W_{s,t}:=\langle s,t\rangle\le W$ be the standard parabolic subgroup, with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$, which agrees with $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2)). For $s\ne t$ and $k\ge0$ let $u_k$ be the alternating word $s\,t\,s\cdots$ of $k$ letters beginning with $s$, so $u_0=1$.

[F5] There is a homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$; hence $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$ for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$. Also $\ell(s)=1$ for every $s\in S$, so $s\ne1$ in $W$. Distinct generators are distinct in $W$, the product $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$, the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{s,t}$ is the Coxeter system presented by the restricted matrix on $\{s,t\}$ with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$ equal to $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$, and every right coset $W_{s,t}a$ has a unique minimal-length representative $d$, characterized by $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$ and satisfying $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_{s,t}$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]]).

The $u_k$ are pairwise distinct: if $u_j=u_k$ with $j<k<2m$, then $1=u_j^{-1}u_k$; for $j,k$ of equal parity this equals $u^{\pm(k-j)/2}$ with $0<(k-j)/2<m$, contradicting the exact order $m$ of $u$ from [F5], while for parities differing it equals $s\,u^{p}$ or $u^{p}s$ with $2|p|<2m$, so it would give $u^{p}=s$, impossible because $\operatorname{sgn}(u^{p})=1$ while $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$. Hence $|W_{s,t}|=2m$, the $u_k$ are distinct, $u_{k+2m}=u_k$, and the pairs $u_k,u_{k+1}$ and $u_{2m-1},u_0$ are edges of the Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for the generating set $\{s,t\}$. That graph is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ because $x

Moreover $su_k=u_{\sigma(k)}$ and $tu_k=u_{	au(k)}$ with $\sigma(k)\equiv1-k\pmod{2m}$ and $	au(k)\equiv-1-k\pmod{2m}$ for $0\le k<2m$: these are $s(st)^{j}=u^{-j}s$, $t(st)^{j}=u^{-j}t=u^{-j-1}s$ applied to $u_{2j}=u^{j}$ and $u_{2j+1}=u^{j}s$, together with the case $k=0$. 1.5 **The infinite dihedral group.** Assume $m(s,t)=\infty$, write $u:=st$, and let $u'_k$ be the alternating word of length $k$ beginning with $t$. By [F5], $u$ has infinite order, and by [F6] $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k=\ell_{s,t}(u'_k)$ for all $k\ge0$. The union $X:=\{u_k:k\ge0\}\cup\{u'_k:k\ge0\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$ ($u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$, $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$, $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$, $u_0t=u'_1$, $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$, symmetrically for $u'_k$), so $X=W_{s,t}$; by [F6] the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k$ for every $k\ge0$, and likewise the $u'_k$. The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$. On the affine line $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$, parametrized by $y_s$, the generators act by $s:y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t:y_s\mapsto 2-y_s$ by [F3] (here $c=1$); consequently the affine map of $u_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s-2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s-2j$ for $k=2j+1$, and that of $u'_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s+2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s+2j+2$ for $k=2j+1$, by induction on $k$ (each step composes with $s$ or $t$ alternately). Hence the trace of $u_kC_P^\circ$ is the interval $(-k,-k+1)$ and that of $u'_kC_P^\circ$ is $(k,k+1)$. Since these intervals are pairwise distinct, an element of $W_{s,t}=X$ is determined by the trace of its chamber. Writing $v_j$ $(j\in\mathbb Z)$ for the element with trace $(j,j+1)$, namely $v_j=u_{-j}$ for $j\le0$ and $v_j=u'_j$ for $j\ge0$, one therefore has $\ell_{s,t}(v_j)=|j|$ together with $s\cdot v_j=v_{-j-1}$ and $t\cdot v_j=v_{1-j}$, because the affine maps send the interval $(j,j+1)$ to $(-j-1,-j)$, respectively $(1-j,2-j)$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

5.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm P)$.** Fix $n\ge0$ and suppose only $(\mathrm Q_n)$. If $S$ is empty there is no $s$ to check. If $S=\{s\}$ then $W=\{1,s\}$ by $s^2=1$ and [F5], and the only positive-length chamber is $sC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$, with $\ell(s)=1$, proving $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$ directly. Now suppose $|S|\ge2$. First $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and (1) imply $(\mathrm P_n)$: for any $a$ of length $n$ and generator $r$, choose $q\ne r$ and use $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to write $a=ud$, with $aC^\circ\subseteq u(B_r\cap B_q)$ and $n=\ell_{r,q}(u)+\ell(d)$. The rank-two dichotomy gives the positive alternative or the negative alternative with $\ell_{r,q}(ru)=\ell_{r,q}(u)-1$; in the latter case $\ell(ra)\le\ell_{r,q}(ru)+\ell(d)=n-1$, hence equality by [F5]. This is $(\mathrm P_n)$. Let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and let $s\in S$; choose $t$ with $w=tw'$ and $\ell(w')=n$. If $s=t$, then $(\mathrm P_n)$ applied to $w'$ gives $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$: the second alternative would give $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=n-1$, whereas $\ell(sw')=\ell(w)=n+1$ here. Hence $wC^\circ=t(w'C^\circ)\subseteq tB_s=sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(w')=n=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. If $s\ne t$, apply $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to $w'$: there is $u\in W_{s,t}$ with $w'C^\circ\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w')=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w')$. Put $v:=tu\in W_{s,t}$. If $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$, then $wC^\circ\subseteq tu(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$. Otherwise $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell_{s,t}(sv)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1$ by (1) from 4.1, so with $d:=u^{-1}w'$ one has $wC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(stu\,d)\le\ell_{s,t}(stu)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1+\ell(d)\le\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(d)=\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$, where $\ell_{s,t}(tu)\le1+\ell_{s,t}(u)$ follows by prepending $t$ to a shortest word for $u$. The reverse bound $\ell(sw)\ge\ell(w)-1$ follows from [F5], so $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. [step 4.1, F3, F5, algebra]

6.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm Q)$.** Suppose $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and $(\mathrm P_m)$ for all $m\le n+1$, as in the second conditional implication of (2), and let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and $s\ne t$. By [F5] factor $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_{s,t}$ and $d$ the minimal representative of $W_{s,t}w$; then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ and $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Since $\ell(d)\le n+1$, $(\mathrm P_{\ell(d)})$ is available: it is part of the stated supposition. Applying it to $d$ and $s'\in\{s,t\}$, the second alternative would give $\ell(s'd)=\ell(d)-1$, contradicting $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$; hence $dC^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$. Therefore $wC^\circ=u(dC^\circ)\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w)$, which is $(\mathrm Q_{n+1})$. [step 5.1, F5, algebra]

8.1 **Part (3).** Let $w\in W$ and $s\ne t$, and factor $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_{s,t}$ and $d$ the minimal representative of $W_{s,t}w$. By [F5], $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ and $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$; since $\ell(d)\le\ell(w)$, $(\mathrm P_{\ell(d)})$ from 7.1 applies to $d$, and the second alternative would give $\ell(s'd)=\ell(d)-1$, a contradiction; hence $dC^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$ and $wC^\circ=u(dC^\circ)\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$, with $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w)$ because $u^{-1}w=d$ and $\ell_{s,t}(u)=\ell(u)$. [step 7.1, F5, algebra]

1.7 **(P_0) and (Q_0).** For $w=1$ one has $\ell(w)=0$, $wC^\circ=C^\circ\subseteq B_r$ for every $r\in S$ by 1.1, and choosing $u=1$ gives $C^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$ and $\ell(1)=0=\ell_{s,t}(1)+\ell(1)$ for all $s\ne t$. [F3, given]

Hence exactly $m$ sectors lie on each side, and the negative side is the contiguous block of $m$ sectors containing $C_1$ but not $C_0$, that is $\{k:y_s<0\text{ on }C_k\}=\{1,\dots,m\}$. 5.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm P)$.** Fix $n\ge0$ and suppose only $(\mathrm Q_n)$. If $S$ is empty there is no $s$ to check. If $S=\{s\}$ then $W=\{1,s\}$ by $s^2=1$ and [F5], and the only positive-length chamber is $sC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$, with $\ell(s)=1$, proving $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$ directly. Now suppose $|S|\ge2$. 9.1 **Converse direction of (4) and conclusion.** Suppose $\ell(sw)<\ell(w)$ and put $w':=sw$, so that $\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$ and $w=sw'$. For $r\in S$ the sets $B_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)>0\}$ and $rB_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)<0\}$ are disjoint and $C^\circ=\bigcap_{r\in S}B_r$; the dual action satisfies $v(B_s\cap B_t)=\{v\cdot f:f\in B_s\cap B_t\}$, and the action of $v\in W_{s,t}$ on $V^*$ is linear. 1.2 **Reduction to the rank-two plane.** Put $C_P^\circ:=\{g\in P^*:g(e_s)>0,\ g(e_t)>0\}$ and let $\pi:V^*\to P^*$, $\pi(f):=f|_P$. Then $\pi$ is linear and surjective, because a functional prescribed on $P$ extends to a functional on $V$ by $0$ on the remaining basis vectors. Every $v\in W_{s,t}$ preserves $P$ and fixes $P^\perp$ pointwise by [F1], so for $x\in P$ and $f\in V^*$ one has $(v\cdot f)(x)=f(\rho(v)^{-1}x)$ with $\rho(v)^{-1}x\in P$; hence $\pi(v\cdot f)=v\cdot\pi(f)$ and $\pi^{-1}(C_P^\circ)=B_s\cap B_t$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}=B_{s'}$, $\pi^{-1}\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}=s'B_{s'}$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Consequently $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})>0\}$, and $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq s'B_{s'}$ if and only if $vC_P^\circ\subseteq\{g:g(e_{s'})<0\}$. [F1, F3, algebra]

The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$.
